definition: Only slightly connected to the main subject or point being discussed.
example: His essay on bridges wandered into tangential remarks about his uncle's fishing boat.
nuance: Tangential means touching a topic only lightly, while irrelevant means having no connection to it at all.
prompt: A student giving a history presentation keeps drifting away from her assigned topic.
options: Her tangential story about a castle tour ate up time meant for the treaty.
She passed around a tangential coin from the era so classmates could hold it.
Her tangential thesis was the main claim that every one of her slides supported.
She gave a tangential answer that addressed exactly what her teacher had asked.
reasons: A story that only brushes against the assigned subject pulls the talk off course.
Something you can physically handle is tangible; this mixes up two look-alike words.
A claim at the heart of the talk is central, the reverse of loosely related.
An answer aimed squarely at the question is on point, not off to the side.

practice.prompt: A book club meets to discuss the surprise ending of a mystery novel.
options: The cover felt tangential, with raised letters you could trace with a fingertip.
A tangential reader finished the novel in a single sitting on Saturday.
One member raised a tangential point about the author's fondness for trains.
The tangential clue that solved the whole case drew most of the group's questions.
reasons: Texture you can feel belongs to tangible things; this confuses similar-sounding words.
The word describes remarks or topics, not how quickly or eagerly someone reads.
The writer's hobby links to the book only loosely, so it drifts from the ending.
A clue that cracks the mystery is essential to the plot, not barely connected.
